solutions.check: grid and clues read from the Guardian's printable copy, its numbering matching the numbers printed in it and the clue list; every fifteensquared answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: HRH upset with promotion such as Lib-Dems' logo?

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and thrown into disorder, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written: His or Her Royal Highness
taken as written

explanation.surface: A royal personage is annoyed that a political party's emblem has been promoted.
explanation.walkthrough: The Liberal Democrats' logo is a stylised bird in flight, the bird of liberty; the question mark flags that it is one example.
explanation.definitionFit: An ornithomorph is a figure or ornament in the shape of a bird, as the party's emblem is.

clue.text: Run off, or run out, one batting?

parts.note: RO is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for run out

indicators.note: batting means hitting about, so the word is knocked into a new order, with the question mark owning up to the stretch

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cricket scene: a batsman is either sent off the field or run out.
explanation.walkthrough: Roneo was a trade name for a stencil duplicating machine, and the verb means to copy with one; the cricket words are all wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To run off copies of a document on a duplicator is to roneo them, a verb taken from the machine's brand name.

clue.text: Musk spilt, empty bottles, flat

indicators.note: to bottle something is to shut it inside, so the word for empty holds the jumbled letters

parts.note: null means void or empty

indicators.note: spilt perfume runs everywhere, so the letters of the scent word are scattered into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Spilt musk perfume and empty bottles lie about a flat, the scene after a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flat' looks like an apartment or a level surface, but in Chambers it is also a noun for a simpleton.
explanation.definitionFit: A flat in the old slang sense is a dupe or simpleton, the same as a dim-witted fool or dunce.

clue.text: Old Bangkok piece that's unconventional? Not …

indicators.note: Not, with the ellipsis carrying on into the next clue, tells you to take away the word that opens that clue

parts.note: heretical means departing from accepted belief, unorthodox

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether an old Thai coin is unusual, and the answer trails off.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis joins this clue to 5 down, whose first word, Present, gives HERE; HERETICAL without HERE leaves TICAL.
explanation.definitionFit: The tical was the former Siamese unit of currency and weight, so an old coin from Bangkok.

clue.text: … Present, mum wrapped, more than one bust

indicators.note: something wrapped is enclosed by an outer covering, so the word for mother sits inside the other word

parts.note: present, as when answering a roll call, means here
ma is an informal word for mother

explanation.surface: A gift for mother has been wrapped, perhaps a pair of sculpted busts.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue continues from 4 down, whose Not takes the same word Present away there.
explanation.definitionFit: Hermae are classical pillars topped with a carved head, originally of Hermes, so a plural of a kind of bust.

clue.text: Astringent shrubs with which doctors will restrict a twitch

indicators.note: to restrict something is to hem it in, so the doctors' letters close around the others

parts.note: MO is medical officer, a military doctor; MOS is the plural
taken as written
a tic is an involuntary twitch

explanation.surface: Doctors prescribe a herbal astringent to control a patient's nervous twitch.
explanation.definitionFit: Matico is a Peruvian shrub whose leaves were used as a styptic, an astringent that stops bleeding.

clue.text: Half of E. African crater upthrust, energy-filled, whence mountains were formed

indicators.note: in a down clue, thrust upward means the letters are read from the bottom up, backwards
filled with something means it is put inside, so the energy letter goes into the middle
half of a long name means only its first five letters are kept and the rest thrown away

parts.note: the Ngorongoro Crater is a huge volcanic caldera in Tanzania
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A geological note on an East African crater pushed up by energy, the place where mountains were formed.
explanation.walkthrough: Ngorongoro conveniently splits into two halves, NGORO and NGORO, so either half serves.
explanation.definitionFit: In geology an orogen is a belt of the earth's crust that has undergone mountain building, the zone that produced a range.

clue.text: Billow, like Britannia at sea, does one hear?

indicators.note: asking whether one hears it says the answer is matched to a spoken word, not a spelt one

parts.note: the Britannia was the British royal yacht, so at sea she was royal

explanation.surface: A question about the waves heaving around the royal yacht Britannia out at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: The sound match only works in an accent that clips royal to one syllable, hence the question mark; Chambers gives the two words different sounds.
explanation.definitionFit: To roil is to churn or surge turbulently, as water or smoke does when it billows.

clue.text: A strong tobacco

parts.note: surface reading: a plain description of a kind of pipe tobacco
setter's reading: there is no wordplay here, because this is the competition word for which solvers write their own clue

explanation.walkthrough: Azed's competition puzzles give the prize word only a bare definition; competitors send in their own cryptic clue for it.
explanation.definitionFit: Perique is a strong, dark, fermented tobacco grown in Louisiana, used mostly in pipe blends.

clue.text: Old club don's left, about to compete for shaggy dog

indicators.note: about means around, so the remaining letters go round the word for compete
the don has left, gone away, so that word is taken out of the club word

parts.note: bourdon is an obsolete word for a pilgrim's staff or club
taken as written, the part removed
to vie is to compete

explanation.surface: At an old club a don has walked out over an entry in a shaggy dog contest.
explanation.walkthrough: Bourdon also names a bell's drone and an organ stop, which hides the old staff sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The bouvier des Flandres is a large Belgian cattle dog with a rough, shaggy coat.

clue.text: Lungfish wriggling in mud below estuarial shoal on river, Australian

indicators.note: in a down clue, below means the following letters sit under the rest in the grid

parts.note: a bar is a bank of sand across a river mouth

indicators.note: something wriggling twists about, so those letters are writhed into a new order

parts.note: R is the map abbreviation for river
A is a standard abbreviation for Australian
taken as written, the letters to be jumbled

explanation.surface: A lungfish squirms in the mud of an Australian river mouth, a fair nature-documentary picture.
explanation.walkthrough: The name is used for more than one Australian fish, including the Queensland lungfish as well as the familiar food fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Barramundi is an Australian name for several fishes, among them the Queensland lungfish, which breathes air.

clue.text: Fine evening star in Italian church niche

parts.note: F is the pencil grading abbreviation for fine
ene is an old dialect word for evening, listed in Chambers
stella is the Italian word for star

explanation.surface: A lovely evening star is seen through a niche in an Italian church.
explanation.definitionFit: A fenestella is a small window-like niche in a church wall beside the altar, holding the piscina.

clue.text: Anger after courts dismantled bureau?

indicators.note: after places the anger word behind the jumbled letters
something dismantled is taken apart, and its letters can be rebuilt in a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written
ire is anger

explanation.surface: There is public anger after the law courts are broken up by an administrative department.
explanation.walkthrough: Bureau suggests a government office; the question mark flags the furniture sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrutoire is an old word for an escritoire, a writing desk, which is what a bureau is in British furniture terms.

clue.text: Letter in Hebrew, pure shmaltz in part

indicators.note: in part says only a portion of the following words is used, a run of letters inside them

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A letter written in Hebrew is described as pure schmaltz, all sentiment.
explanation.walkthrough: Schmaltz, Yiddish for chicken fat and so for sentimentality, fits the Hebrew setting.
explanation.definitionFit: Resh is the twentieth letter of the Hebrew alphabet, equivalent to R.

clue.text: Sexually incomplete male squirmin' by the sound of it

indicators.note: by the sound of it says the word is matched as spoken, not as spelt

parts.note: squirming is wriggling, with the dropped g shown by the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A male animal that has not been fully castrated squirms uncomfortably.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in squirmin' tells you the matching word also drops its final g.
explanation.definitionFit: A riglin, a form of ridgel, is a male animal with an undescended testicle, or one imperfectly castrated.

clue.text: All right being in shift? Such a short cloak's not worn these days

definitions.text: Such a short cloak's not worn these days
definitions.note: the whole phrase defines it: a short cloak, now obsolete

indicators.note: being in something means placed inside it, so the all-right letters sit within the shift word

parts.note: a relay is a shift or fresh team of workers taking over
OK means all right

explanation.surface: Is it fine to wear this short cloak on a shift? Nobody wears one now.
explanation.walkthrough: Shift also suggests a loose dress, which pulls toward clothing; here it is a spell of work.
explanation.definitionFit: A rokelay is an obsolete Scots word for a short cloak, so a garment no longer worn.

clue.text: Temple at Teotihuacan? Old name I found under site, half removed

indicators.note: in a down clue, found under puts the shortened word below the rest
with half removed, only the second two of its four letters stay

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for old
to name someone is to call them something
taken as written
taken as written; its first half is dropped

explanation.surface: An archaeologist names an old temple found buried under a half-cleared Mexican site.
explanation.walkthrough: The blocks are listed top to bottom but the site remnant goes first, since everything else is found under it.
explanation.definitionFit: A teocalli is an Aztec or Mesoamerican temple on a stepped pyramid, the kind at Teotihuacan near Mexico City.

clue.text: First to last, ban approach to border

definitions.note: a verb: to come up against and touch

indicators.note: First to last says the opening letter moves to the end, rotating the word

parts.note: tabu is a variant spelling of taboo, a ban

explanation.surface: An instruction that leading people must go to the back, with a ban on approaching the frontier.
explanation.definitionFit: To abut is to adjoin, so things that come right up to a border and touch it are adjacent at it.

clue.text: Rude name for frump with wobbly rear creating rumpus

parts.note: old bag is a rude term for a dowdy or unattractive woman

indicators.note: something wobbly shakes unsteadily, so those letters are shaken into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be jumbled

explanation.surface: An insult about a dowdy woman's wobbling backside starts a row.
explanation.definitionFit: Bagarre is a French loan word in Chambers for a scuffle or brawl, a noisy uproar.

clue.text: Ace evident in super flexed leg muscle

indicators.note: evident in means seen inside, so the ace word sits within the other letters
something flexed is bent out of its line, so those letters are reshaped

parts.note: taken as written, to be jumbled
an ace is a one in cards and dice

explanation.surface: A star athlete shows off a superbly flexed leg muscle.
explanation.walkthrough: Ace and super both read as praise for an athlete, but one is a number and the other is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The peroneus muscles run down the outer side of the lower leg and move the foot.

clue.text: Back parts of insects are mostly on top when flying

indicators.note: things flying are tossed about in the air, so the letters land in a new order
mostly means all but a little, so the final letter goes

parts.note: taken as written, then shortened
taken as written

explanation.surface: An entomologist notes that the backs of insects are mostly uppermost in flight.
explanation.definitionFit: A pronotum is the upper plate of an insect's first thoracic segment, its back; pronota is the plural.

clue.text: Kids frequenting shopping center in millions? Complete phooey! (8, two words)

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for million
complete means whole, all
rats! is an exclamation of disgust, like phooey!

explanation.surface: Millions of youngsters hang around shopping centres; someone dismisses the idea as nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: The US spelling center matches the American origin of the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Mall rats is American slang for teenagers who spend their free time loitering in shopping malls.

clue.text: Old record as found in one pressing?

indicators.note: found in means located inside, so the example abbreviation sits within the other word

parts.note: a lier is one that lies, here taken as lying flat and pressing down
as, in the sense of for example, is e.g.

explanation.surface: An old gramophone record found at a pressing plant.
explanation.walkthrough: Pressing points to vinyl records; but the record here is a book of accounts, and the word is an obsolete spelling of ledger.
explanation.definitionFit: Lieger is an old form of ledger, the book in which a business keeps its record of accounts.

clue.text: Getting hot in a jiffy, Father William answered youth so

indicators.note: getting something means taking it in, so the heat letter is received inside the other word

parts.note: in a jiffy means in a trice, so a jiffy is a trice
H is the tap abbreviation for hot

explanation.surface: Father William loses his temper quickly at a young man's questions.
explanation.walkthrough: In Lewis Carroll's poem You Are Old, Father William, from Alice in Wonderland, the old man says 'I have answered three questions, and that is enough'.
explanation.definitionFit: Father William answered the youth three times before refusing more, so he answered on three occasions.

clue.text: One such, to love denied?

parts.note: Edgar Allan Poe is one example of the kind of writer the answer names

indicators.note: denied means refused or deprived, so the word loses the letter for love

parts.note: taken as written
love is nil in tennis, so O; it is the letter removed

explanation.surface: The romantic figure of the lovelorn versifier, a type famously denied love.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: Poe is one such writer, and the stereotype of the lovesick lyricist is the definition; the question mark admits the cliché.
explanation.definitionFit: Writers of verse are proverbially lovesick and unrequited, so the whole clue paints a typical one.

clue.text: Nasty swelling: start of remedy's involved in risk

indicators.note: involved in means wrapped up inside, so that letter goes within the risk word

parts.note: to take a risk is to take a chance

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter, which is all that is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of remedy

explanation.surface: A doctor warns that treating a nasty swelling involves some risk.
explanation.definitionFit: A chancre is a hard sore or lesion, typically the first sign of syphilis, so a nasty raised spot.

clue.text: A head of state inspiring ridicule? Yes and (possibly) no

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, which is the only one used

parts.note: the opening letter of state
sad in modern slang means pathetic, worthy of mockery
surface padding: a wry aside answering the question, giving no letters

explanation.surface: Is a certain president a figure of fun? The setter answers yes and perhaps no.
explanation.walkthrough: A head of state is both the definition and, read letter by letter, the first two pieces. The tail is a wry aside: the slang sense of sad fits, the everyday sense of sorrowful may not.
explanation.definitionFit: Bashar al-Assad was President of Syria when the puzzle appeared, so a head of state.

clue.text: Some anachronistic errors turned up in narrative

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned up means read from the bottom upward, backwards
some means a portion of the following words, a run of letters inside them

parts.note: the letters straddle the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Some anachronisms have been spotted in a historical novel.
explanation.definitionFit: A recit is a narrative, especially the text or story of a book as against its illustrations; Chambers lists it.

clue.text: Notice penned by rare bird: it includes Tlingit

indicators.note: penned by means shut in by, as an animal in a pen, so the notice word sits within the bird's

parts.note: the nene is the Hawaiian goose, once close to extinction
an ad is an advertisement, a notice

explanation.surface: A notice is written by a rare bird and includes something in Tlingit.
explanation.walkthrough: Tlingit is a Native language of south-east Alaska; the colon marks the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Na-Dene is the North American language family that takes in Tlingit, the Athabaskan languages and Haida.

clue.text: Brushlike tail of Reynard behind

indicators.note: the tail of a word is its final letter, which is all that is kept

parts.note: the final letter of Reynard, the fox of fable
aft means behind, at the stern

explanation.surface: A fox's bushy tail, a brush, is at the back.
explanation.walkthrough: A fox's tail is called its brush, which pulls toward a literal reading; the definition comes from the British phrase daft as a brush, meaning very silly.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'as a brush' attaches to silliness, so being like a brush in the saying means being foolish.

clue.text: Chinese ounce; also Scottish pound

parts.note: tae is the Scots form of too, meaning also
L, from Latin libra, is the abbreviation for a pound

explanation.surface: A list of old weights: a Chinese ounce, and also a Scottish pound.
explanation.definitionFit: The tael was a Chinese unit of weight of about an ounce and a third, also used for silver money.

clue.text: Watch unremittingly to continue tediously, that is including seconds

parts.note: to drag on is to go on wearisomely

indicators.note: including means taking in, so the abbreviation for that is goes round the seconds letter

parts.note: i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is
s is the abbreviation for seconds

explanation.surface: Keeping watch without a break makes the time pass slowly, second by second.
explanation.definitionFit: To dragonise is to guard watchfully like a dragon over a hoard, keeping constant vigil.

clue.text: A glacis quarried for limestone

indicators.note: something quarried is dug out and broken up, so the letters come out in pieces to be reassembled

parts.note: taken as written; a glacis is a defensive slope before a fortification

explanation.surface: A fortress slope is being dug out to supply building stone.
explanation.definitionFit: Scaglia is a reddish or white Italian chalky limestone, a particular type of the rock.

clue.text: Type of copper ore Mad Hatter tried mixing with earth

indicators.note: mixing stirs things together, so all the letters are blended into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
E is the abbreviation for earth

explanation.surface: Alice's Mad Hatter experiments with blending copper ore and soil, a tea-party chemistry lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: Mad is part of the character's name from Alice in Wonderland and reads like a second signal, but the letters come from Hatter alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Tetrahedrite is a grey mineral, a copper antimony sulphide, which is mined as an ore of copper.
